stories.title: Volcano eruption triggers flight suspensions at Indonesia's main airport
stories.summary: A volcanic eruption has halted hundreds of flights at Indonesia's main international airport, stranding tens of thousands of passengers. Authorities said 209 flights were suspended after ash from Mount Anak Krakatoa was detected in airspace near Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Sunday morning. The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said. More than 22,000 people have been impacted by the suspension of flights, which has been extended until 13:30 (0630 GMT). The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur. Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra. The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks. Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa. Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where there is high volcanic and seismic activity.

stories.title: RSPB marks 50 years at wildlife-rich reserve
stories.summary: A nature reserve tucked away on the Broads and home to some of Norfolk's most threatened wildlife is celebrating 50 years. Strumpshaw Fen covers 450 hectares (1,112 acres) of diverse wetland — the equivalent of 630 football pitches. Reserves manager Helen Deavin said the site supported "rare and unusual species", including nesting bitterns, the swallowtail butterfly and a pair of cranes that successfully raised a chick this summer. "One of the lovely things about Strumpshaw is that the wildlife is quite accessible," added Deavin, who called the reserve a "hidden gem". Marsh harriers, bearded tits, flocks of waders and overwintering ducks and geese are a regular sight for visitors, along with otters, water voles, fen raft spiders, orchids and rare sharp-leaved pondweed. "There's this incredible, really quite rare wildlife but actually it's really possible for people to see it, get some great views and really experience the magic of the Broads," added Deavin. "By developing habitats where wildlife feels safe and can find the right food and places to shelter and raise a family, teams across the years have created a reserve that helps populations of rare species not only survive, but thrive." She said the summer's heatwaves had been "tough", but they were hoping for a cooler, wetter autumn, with the reserve braced for flood events and "saline surges" with seasonal tides. Strumpshaw is hosting various events to celebrate the milestone, including guided walks around the site on Sunday. The reserve started off as unmanaged fenland and was taken over by the RSPB in the mid-1970s. BBC Look East camera operator. Shaun Whitmore has always loved Strumpshaw Fen and in his own words, he explains why.
